title: Nearly 40% of 2025 Budget short of substantial implementation: Verité Research | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 05:45
-     - 78

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake

Nearly 40%, that is 14 of 36 high-value proposals, in Sri Lanka’s 2025 Budget fell short of substantial implementation, according to the latest Budget Promises assessment by Verité Research.

At the same time, the share of fulfilled proposals increased from 17% in 2024 to 33% in 2025, marking the highest rate recorded since Verité Research began tracking Budget implementation in 2017. Overall, 41% (15 proposals) were either fulfilled or substantially implemented. 

The improvement came despite a shorter-than-usual implementation window, as the Budget was presented in February 2025.

Another 19% (7 proposals) lacked sufficient information to assess progress and were classified as undisclosed.

The assessment tracked 36 high-value proposals, each valued at Rs. 500 million or more, collectively accounting for Rs. 212 billion in allocations. 

Openness also showed notable progress. Nearly two-thirds of proposals (64%) were rated open. For the first time since 2017, no proposal was rated closed. That means, at least some information was available about every proposal, even when it was not adequate to evaluate progress. 

Budget Promises is a dashboard under publicfinance.lk maintained by Verité Research that tracks the implementation of proposals made in Sri Lanka’s annual Budget speeches since 2017.

Detailed progress on each Budget Promise can be found on the dashboard at https://dashboards.publicfinance.lk/budget-promises/.

title: President sends expectations  sky-high ahead of Thursday’s Budget | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 05:44
-     - 91

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake has raised expectations of fresh tax relief in Thursday’s Budget, saying the Government expects to lift the Pay As You Earn (PAYE) tax threshold again. PAYE is income tax deducted at source from salaries.

Addressing the National Trade Union Convention in Colombo on Saturday, the President said the threshold had already been increased from Rs. 100,000 to Rs. 150,000 and that a further adjustment to it was expected in the 2027 Budget, to be presented to Parliament on Thursday.

President Dissanayake said discussions had been held with private sector institutions and business associations, following which basic salaries were raised. He acknowledged that higher basic pay alone was insufficient to give employees meaningful financial relief and said supplementary allowances had also been considered.

He said PAYE deductions on higher salaries remained an important concern, and that the Government had a responsibility to protect the interests and economic security of employees across the State, semi-Government, plantation, and private sectors.

President Dissanayake has set out a string of tax and spending relief measures ahead of Thursday’s Budget, from a staged reduction in Value Added Tax (VAT) to a further increase in the PAYE threshold, while conceding the pledges must be squared with a rising salary bill.

Addressing a ceremony at Temple Trees on 8 October where appointment letters were issued to 1,540 Grama Niladhari officers, the President set out a multi-year cut in the VAT rate. “Our objective is to provide relief to the people by reducing VAT rates over the next two to three years,” he said.

He also called for the removal of taxes on essential educational materials. “If a child has to pay a tax when purchasing a book to read, we should remove that tax,” he said.

At a rally in Gampaha on 4 October, President Dissanayake said a property tax on houses proposed under the International Monetary Fund (IMF) program had been deferred for another year. The Government has told the IMF that revenue measures planned for the Budget would be sufficient to meet targets, making the tax unnecessary.

At a rally in Akuressa on 20 September, he said the Government would remove certain taxes in the Budget and had set aside Rs. 2 billion for capital expenditure at the grassroots level. 

The Budget will also strengthen public healthcare to cut the cost of private treatment, the President said in July, and will fund 750 communication towers next year towards a target of 1,000 in three years, Grade Six education reforms, and an electric train project.

The pledges sit against a three-stage public sector basic salary increase that the President said would cost an additional Rs. 330 billion by 2027. Revenue is required to stay above 15.3% and 15.4% of GDP in 2026 and 2027 under the debt restructuring, and the Government has locked in a primary expenditure ceiling of 12.9% of GDP. The IMF program ends in March 2027, with debt service stepping up in 2028.

The Government maintains the Budget will stay within IMF parameters. Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya told Parliament on 9 October that public sector salaries would rise through the Budget.

title: Lanka Realty Investments bolsters future growth with two top British experts on Board | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 05:40
-     - 56

Lanka Realty Investments PLC (LRI) has announced the appointment of two top British personalities to its Board as Independent Non-Executive Directors in a move to bolster the company’s future growth trajectory. 

The two members are veteran banker of HSBC-fame Mark Prothero and top UK real estate specialist Piers Charles Kirshaw Rooke.

Prothero is an accomplished and experienced banking executive covering enterprise-wide risk management, internal audit, and business management.

He has held senior leadership positions across Asia, the Middle East, Europe, and the Americas in a distinguished 31-year career with the HSBC Group as an International Manager. During the period September 2016 to September 2021, he was the CEO of HSBC Sri Lanka and the Maldives. He also served as a Non-Executive Director of HSBC Mauritius and the President of the British Chamber of Commerce in Sri Lanka.

Prothero has chaired Risk and Audit Committees within the HSBC Group both in an Executive and Non-Executive capacity. In addition to his many years of diverse banking experience, he is also a certified anti-money laundering specialist.

Rooke is a UK property investor, developer, and asset manager with over 25 years’ experience as a principal in the commercial and residential real estate sectors in the UK and Europe.

He is CEO of Castlecap Investments Management Ltd., a privately owned prosperity group that invests in, develops, and manages office, retail, industrial, leisure, student, and residential property across the UK. During his career, he has been directly involved in over £ 1.2 billion of property transactions. He has founded and led four property businesses as a Founding Shareholder – Waterbridge Investment Partners, Seastar Developments, Ebberly Investments, and Castlecap Investments – investing on behalf of institutional and private investors, and building a privately owned UK-focussed real estate investment and development business.

Rooke’s experience spans the full investment cycle; acquisition, structuring and financing, planning and development, asset management, and disposal. He began his career in the London financial markets.

LRI also announced that Independent Non-Executive Directors Sarravanan Neelakandan and Mohamed Firdouse Farook will become Non-Independent Non-Executive Directors following their completion of nine years of service on the Board.

Prothero and Rooke have been appointed to the LRI Audit Committee, Remuneration Committee, Related Party Transactions Review Committee, and Nominations and Governance Committee.

With the latest appointments, the Board of Directors of LRI comprises S. Neelakandan (Chairman), M.H. Jamaldeen, A.J.B. Warman, M.F. Farook, B.V. Selvanayagam, P. Morgan, Mark Prothero, and Piers Rooke.

title: JAAF welcomes Govt.’s stance on securing long-term access to EU market | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 05:39
-     - 35

The Joint Apparel Association Forum (JAAF) yesterday said it appreciates the Government’s commitment to submitting a fresh application for the EU’s Generalised Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+) scheme under the new 10-year trade framework.

“For Sri Lanka’s apparel industry, GSP+ is more than a tariff concession. It supports the competitiveness of our exporters in our largest market and sustains the livelihoods of hundreds of thousands of workers and their families. Continued access is vital to the industry and to the wider economy,” the JAAF said in a 

statement.

The JAAF also welcomed the Government’s two-pronged approach: securing continued GSP+ benefits under the revised framework, while examining alternative arrangements that could offer more sustainable, long-term access to the European market. This balance of immediate protection and forward planning is what the sector needs, and it gives exporters and investors the confidence to plan ahead.

The JAAF recognises that Sri Lanka’s ability to complete the reapplication process and meet the updated eligibility and compliance requirements will be crucial to maintaining its preferential position in the EU in the years ahead. The industry stands ready to play its part. 

“We will continue to uphold high standards of labour practice, environmental stewardship, and good governance, which are the values at the heart of the scheme and of our industry’s reputation with global buyers,” the JAAF said.

Apparel remains Sri Lanka’s largest export earner. In 2025, the sector’s exports crossed $ 5 billion, contributing about 32% of the country’s total export earnings of $ 17.25 billion and over half of its industrial exports. The EU, which takes up 24% of Sri Lanka’s merchandise exports, is central to this performance. Continued GSP+ access therefore matters greatly to the industry, its workforce, and the national economy.

“The JAAF looks forward to working closely with the Government and all relevant stakeholders to ensure a smooth and timely application, and to strengthening Sri Lanka’s long-term partnership with the EU,” it said.

title: Official reserves top $ 7 b in Oct., CBSL ups dollar buying with $ 191 m | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 05:39
-     - 61

Official reserve assets topped the $ 7 billion mark at end-October, Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) data showed, as the monetary authority increased US dollar purchases from the domestic foreign exchange market. 

Official reserves stood at $ 7.09 billion at end-October 2026, up from $ 6.9 billion a month earlier, while foreign currency reserves rose to $ 6.84 billion from $ 6.62 billion.

The $ 190 million increase in official reserves almost matches the $ 191.3 million the CBSL bought on a net basis during October, a month in which it made no sales.

Expected short-term outflows, covering the forward leg of currency swaps and loan servicing, amount to $ 5.75 billion, CBSL data showed. That is equivalent to 84% of foreign currency reserves and leaves about $ 1.09 billion free of near-term drains, with reserves covering committed outflows around 1.2 times. The forward leg is the side of a currency swap that falls due.

October’s $ 191.3 million net purchase was the largest since August but remained 67% below the record $ 579 million bought that month, and was nearly triple September’s $ 64.2 million. September’s figure was the smallest monthly purchase since the CBSL resumed buying in June with $ 70.5 million, after it sold a net $ 12.9 million in April and $ 211.3 million in May.

The rupee came under its heaviest pressure in that period after the conflict in the Middle East escalated in late February, with year-to-date (YTD) depreciation peaking at 7.9% at end-June. Purchases then accelerated to $ 348.6 million in July and the record $ 579 million in August, the highest single month since January 2025, as the rupee recovered and YTD depreciation eased to 7.8% at end-July and 5.5% at end-August.

September’s buying took net purchases for the first nine months of 2026 above $ 1.54 billion, against $ 2 billion for the whole of 2025. October’s addition lifts the 10-month total above $ 1.73 billion, leaving the CBSL within roughly $ 270 million of last year’s full-year figure with two months remaining.

title: Private credit rebounds in Sept., but growth slows a third month | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 05:38
-     - 59

Private sector borrowing from Sri Lanka’s banking system rebounded in September from August’s four-month low, though annual growth slowed for a third consecutive month. 

This is according to Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) data released last Friday. Net credit expanded Rs. 212.4 billion month-on-month (MoM), provisional CBSL data showed. Outstanding credit to the private sector rose to Rs. 11.77 trillion from Rs. 11.56 trillion in August, while year-on-year (YoY) growth eased to 23.6% from 24.5%.

The September increase was nonetheless 6.4% below the Rs. 226.8 billion added in September 2025, the second consecutive month in which monthly borrowing ran below the year-earlier level. Annual growth has now decelerated for three straight months, from 26.4% in July. Since June 2025, monthly additions have ranged from Rs. 83 billion in January to Rs. 263 billion in November 2025, with a trough of Rs. 101 billion in April.

Lending by Domestic Banking Units (DBUs), which handle rupee business, rose Rs. 171.8 billion to Rs. 11.17 trillion, up from Rs. 138.7 billion in August, though YoY growth eased to 25% from 26.6%. Credit from Offshore Banking Units (OBUs), which handle banks’ foreign currency business, added Rs. 40.6 billion to Rs. 597.9 billion, reversing August’s Rs. 33.1 billion contraction. OBU credit stood 2.1% above the year-earlier level, down from 6.5% growth in August.

Net credit to the Government from the banking system fell Rs. 84.8 billion to Rs. 7.65 trillion, with the YoY contraction little changed at 7.6% from 7.7%. The decline was split between the two lender groups, in contrast to August when it came entirely from the CBSL. Net CBSL credit to the Government fell Rs. 32.8 billion to Rs. 1.4 trillion, a 22.1% YoY contraction, while commercial bank credit fell Rs. 52 billion to Rs. 6.25 trillion.

Outstanding credit to public corporations and State-Owned Business Enterprises (SOBEs) declined Rs. 16.9 billion to Rs. 462.9 billion, widening the YoY contraction to 24% from 22.3%.

Net foreign assets (NFA) of the banking system, its foreign assets minus foreign liabilities, fell Rs. 41.9 billion to Rs. 1.63 trillion, the first monthly decline in the series since the start of the year. Commercial banks’ Net Foreign Assets (NFA) dropped Rs. 82.2 billion to Rs. 515.4 billion, offsetting a Rs. 40.3 billion rise in the CBSL’s NFA to Rs. 1.12 trillion. YoY growth in system NFA slowed to 69.2% from 67.5%. Net domestic assets rose Rs. 90.6 billion to Rs. 15.56 trillion, with YoY growth easing to 7.3% from 7.6%.

On monetary aggregates, reserve money, the cash base banks hold with the CBSL, rose Rs. 39 billion to Rs. 1.95 trillion, and YoY growth accelerated to 15.2% from 11.8%. M1, the narrowest measure of money covering currency and demand deposits, fell Rs. 33.8 billion to Rs. 2.36 trillion, with YoY growth easing to 11.2% from 12.6%. M2 rose Rs. 53.9 billion to Rs. 15.09 trillion and M2b, the broadest measure, rose Rs. 48.7 billion to Rs. 17.19 trillion, with YoY growth easing to 10.6% and 11.1%, respectively.

title: Record workers’ remittances in Oct., first 10 months | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 05:38
-     - 84

Workers’ remittances surged to a record high in October, driving one of the strongest 10-month performances in the country’s history, despite heightened economic uncertainty from the ongoing Middle East conflict, a region that hosts a large share of Sri Lankan migrant workers.

Latest data from the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) showed that inflows rose 3.31% year-on-year (YoY) to $ 735.6 million. October marked the ninth consecutive month of exceptionally strong remittance inflows, highlighting the continued resilience of Sri Lankan migrant workers and the growing use of formal transfer channels.

Cumulative remittances for the first 10 months of 2026 also rose to over $ 7.6 billion, registering a robust 16.5% YoY increase and marking the strongest January-October performance in Sri Lanka’s history.

With export earnings and tourism facing external pressures, remittances have once again reinforced their position as Sri Lanka’s single largest source of foreign exchange, providing critical support to external reserves and broader macroeconomic stability.

The strong start to the year follows a historic performance in 2025, when full-year remittances climbed to $ 8.07 billion, a 23% increase from a year earlier and the highest annual inflow ever recorded. 

The total exceeded the previous all-time high of $ 7.24 billion in 2016 by about 12%, firmly cementing remittances as Sri Lanka’s largest and most reliable source of foreign exchange during its ongoing post-crisis recovery.

CBSL data show that the rebound has been both sharp and sustained since the collapse in inflows during the 2022 economic crisis, when remittances fell 31% to a 12-year low of $ 3.78 billion amid acute foreign exchange shortages and the proliferation of informal transfer channels. 

The turnaround began in 2023, when inflows surged 57% to $ 5.96 billion, marking the strongest post-crisis recovery on record. 

Momentum continued in 2024, with remittances rising a further 10.1% YoY to $ 6.57 billion, supported by a wave of outbound labour migration as thousands of Sri Lankans sought overseas employment in the aftermath of the economic collapse. 

Historically, Sri Lanka’s workers’ remittances averaged around $ 7 billion a year between 2014 and 2018, or roughly $ 600 million a month, reinforcing their longstanding role as a stabilising pillar of the economy.

title: SENOK celebrates 47 years of enterprise, innovation and nation building | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 05:32
-     - 32

SENOK is marking its 47th anniversary this year, celebrating nearly five decades of Sri Lankan enterprise and growth across industries that have played an important role in the country’s development.

From a travel company established in 1979, SENOK has grown into one of Sri Lanka’s largest diversified privately owned business groups, today encompassing more than 40 companies with interests spanning construction and heavy machinery, automobiles and commercial vehicles, renewable energy, manufacturing and aviation, with operations extending beyond Sri Lanka into international markets.

SENOK was founded in 1979 by Noel Selvanayagam with the establishment of Senok Travels Ltd. From its beginnings in the travel industry, the business soon expanded into construction machinery and began the diversification that would shape the Group over the decades that followed. As SENOK grew, Managing Director Gerard Fernando became a key force in its development, playing a central role in building and leading many of the Group’s principal businesses, operations and major projects.

Construction and heavy machinery became one of the foundations of the Group’s growth. Machinery supplied and supported by SENOK has been deployed across roads, irrigation schemes, hydropower projects, precast construction projects, harbours, airports and other major infrastructure throughout Sri Lanka. Today, SENOK represents internationally recognised brands including Kobelco, JCB, HAMM and Airman, supported by extensive sales, service, spare parts and technical capabilities.

The Group subsequently established a significant presence in automobiles and commercial vehicles. Its current portfolio includes CHANGAN, DEEPAL, NEVO, GWM, FOTON and EICHER, spanning passenger vehicles, SUVs, pickups, commercial vehicles and new-energy mobility. Through Western Automobile Assembly (WAA) in Kuliyapitiya, SENOK has also invested in local vehicle assembly, contributing to local value addition, employment, technical knowledge transfer and skills development.

SENOK was also the pioneer of wind power development in Sri Lanka, helping introduce commercial wind generation to the country long before renewable energy became a national priority. Its energy interests have since expanded into hydro and solar power, with capabilities covering project development, engineering, construction, commissioning, operation and maintenance.

Aviation represents another distinctive chapter in the Group’s history. In 2012, SENOK expanded into aviation with the establishment of Senok Air, operating Airbus AS350 B3 multi-role helicopters across specialised aviation services including passenger transport, aerial filming, mapping and survey work and medical evacuations. Supported by its own engineering and maintenance capabilities and an experienced flying crew, Senok Air has developed a specialised helicopter operation serving both commercial and critical-response requirements across Sri Lanka.

Beyond Sri Lanka, SENOK has established a growing international presence, including in the Maldives and East and West Africa, extending its experience and capabilities in construction, machinery, commercial vehicles and other sectors into overseas markets.

While much of SENOK’s growth has taken place away from the public eye, its businesses have been closely connected with Sri Lanka’s development for decades – helping build infrastructure, pioneering renewable energy, introducing international technologies, developing local manufacturing capability and creating skilled employment.

SENOK said as it enters its 48th year, it does so with the same willingness to enter new industries, take on ambitious projects and build businesses for the long term that has defined the Group since 1979.

title: Venkadeshwara Agro unveils Board to drive next phase of growth | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 05:13
-     - 65

Venkadeshwara Agro Industry Ltd., the largest edible oil manufacturer in Sri Lanka’s Northern Province, has constituted a seven-member Board of Directors that pairs founder leadership with deep expertise in banking, finance, FMCG, exports and sustainability. 

Five of the seven directors are independent, a structure that signals the Company’s intent to hold itself to the governance standards expected of Sri Lanka’s leading corporates as it scales. 

The appointment  of Michael Ranasinghe and L. Chiranthi Cooray to Venkadeshwara’s Board has strengthened the company’s existing robust leadership which includes Dr. Bradley Emerson (Non-Executive Chairman), Kanakasingam Suganthon (Founder/MD), Rizvi Mowlana, R. Suresh, and Manjula Priyadarshana. 

L. Chiranthi Cooray, is appointed as an Independent Board Director and specialist in ESG, Enterprise Transformation and Risk Expert. She is the Founder, of Accedo Intel. 

With more than 20 years of leadership experience across banking, financial services, capital markets, the public sector, and academia. Chiranthi brings a strong combination of board governance, enterprise risk, ESG, human capital, organisational transformation, and institutional resilience expertise. Her work focuses on helping boards and senior leadership teams strengthen accountability, culture, leadership capability, internal controls, and sustainable performance. 

Michael Ranasinghe is appointed as an Independent Non-Executive Director. He boasts of dual qualifications in marketing and digital marketing and a MBA from UK with International experience in marketing, management and strategic advisory, including 11 years with a Japanese multinational, senior management with a Hong Kong-based fashion house, an educator and co-founder of Synergy School of Business London, currently serving on the board of an international health tech company and consultant to multiple boards.

Venkadeshwara Agro Industry Founder and Managing Director Kanakasingam Suganthon said: “We started this journey in Jaffna in 2001 with a simple belief: that the North could produce oils as good as any on a Sri Lankan table. Today our refinery supplies households, bakeries and food manufacturers. This Board gives us the experience to take the next step, with more capacity, stronger brands and new markets overseas, without losing the quality and the community that got us here.”

With its Board in place, the Company’s priorities include expanding production and marketing capacity, building its consumer and bakery-ingredient brands, deepening its presence in export markets, and developing its laboratory into a center offering third-party quality testing to businesses across Sri Lanka.

“Venkadeshwara is driven towards a stronger governance, financial discipline culture with market insight that allows the business to standout. With five independent directors and experience that spans banking, finance, FMCG and exports, we intend to hold ourselves to the standards that investors, lenders and customers expect of the country’s best-run companies,” said Non-Executive Chairman Dr. Bradley Emerson.

Venkadeshwara’s journey began in 2001, and it was incorporated as a limited liability company in 2014. In 2018 it commissioned its refinery in the Achchuveli Industrial Zone, Jaffna, and is today one of the largest edible oil refining and solvent extraction facilities in the Northern Province, with annual capacity of 17,000 tons of oil refining and 30,000 tons of solvent extraction. In 2021 the Company received a Rs. 100 million grant under the World Bank’s Sri Lanka Agriculture Sector Modernisation Project. It directly employs more than 100 people in the region.

The Company manufactures premium (RBD) palm olein, coconut oil and rice bran oil, and has expanded into margarine and bakery fats in 2025. Nothing is wasted: by-products are converted into palm, coconut and rice fatty acids, rice bran wax, palm stearin and, serving food manufacturers, bakeries and industrial users. A pioneer of advanced filtration technology in edible oil refining in the Jaffna District, Venkadeshwara is ISO 9001:2015, HACCP, GMP and Halal certified, with an in-house laboratory and quality control at every stage of production.

Dr. Bradley Emerson, Non-Executive Chairman is a seasoned senior banker and management professional with more than four decades of experience in strategic leadership across private and public sector boards, including a banking career spanning Commercial Bank, Nations Trust Bank and Pan Asia Bank, and service as CIMA Regional Director for the Middle East, South Asia and North Africa.

Kanakasingam Suganthon, Founder and Managing Director is the entrepreneur who built Venkadeshwara from its Jaffna roots into one of the North’s leading manufacturers, and who continues to set its strategic direction.

Rizvi Mowlana, Marketing Director, brings more than four decades in FMCG marketing, with deep knowledge of consumer markets, brands and commercial strategy.

R. Suresh, Independent Non-Executive Director, is a Chartered Accountant, Chartered Management Accountant with over 20 years of experience in the field of taxation , and Principal at Gajma and Co., bringing strength in accounting, taxation and financial oversight.

Manjula Priyadarshana, Independent Non-Executive Director is a CIMA member with 22 years across the FMCG and export sectors.

title: Dialog Pay wins Gold for Best Digital Payments Innovation at Sri Lanka FinTech Awards 2026 | Daily FT

Dialog Axiata PLC, Sri Lanka’s #1 connectivity provider, won the Gold Award for Best Digital Payments Innovation at the Sri Lanka FinTech Awards 2026, recognising Dialog Pay’s contribution to strengthening Sri Lanka’s national digital payments ecosystem by making secure, convenient, and accessible digital transactions available to consumers and businesses across the country. 

Launched earlier this year, Dialog Pay brings together a comprehensive range of everyday financial transactions through the MyDialog platform and the dedicated Dialog Pay App. Customers can make QR payments, pay bills, transfer money, link bank accounts, access GovPay services and selected financial services through a single digital platform. In a short span of time, Dialog Pay has expanded its QR payment acceptance footprint to more than 100,000 outlets across Sri Lanka, enabling seamless digital transactions for customers while helping merchants participate more actively in the country’s growing digital payments landscape.

Dialog Axiata PLC Group Chief Executive Supun Weerasinghe said: “As Sri Lanka’s digital economy continues to evolve, trusted and accessible digital payments solutions will play an increasingly important role in connecting people, businesses, and services. title: Shared responsibility key to protecting elections from disinformation | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 05:25
-     - 19

Representatives of the Election Commission of Sri Lanka (ECSL), the media, and civil society met in Colombo on 30 October to discuss how to protect the integrity of election information. Democracy Reporting International (DRI) organised the event, Beyond the Algorithm, under the project Strengthening Resilience Against Disinformation in Sri Lanka. The European Union co-funds the project.

Opening the event, DRI Executive Director Nicola Schmidt said that disinformation is a worldwide phenomenon. 

“Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a big issue. Deepfakes and disinformation are being spread through different channels. Social media and different platforms are contributing to the speed of the spread of disinformation. We as DRI are looking into this globally, looking at what algorithms do. That’s why the title of this conference is Beyond the Algorithm. It’s not just the algorithms but their contributions to disinformation is very important when promoting digital rights and trying to hold tech platforms accountable for what they are doing,” she said.

Addressing the gathering, ECSL Member A.M. Faaiz said that algorithms decide what appears on our screen, but algorithms do not vote. 

“Behind every screen sits a citizen and behind every ballot lies a judgement that citizen has formed from what he or she has read, heard, and come to believe. Our concern is with the quality of the judgement and with the conditions with which it was formed. Democracy rests on a simple promise; that citizens are free to choose and that their choice is an informed one,” he said. 

Faaiz further said that with the support of DRI and Factum, the ECSL is formulating a strategic action plan on disinformation and harmful content and mapping digital capacities to shape a roadmap for the Commission’s digital presence. 

“What began as a project is becoming part of the institution. Our purpose is to protect the voters, not to police opinion. Every measure we take must remain consistent with freedom of expression and media freedom. Protecting electoral integrity must never become a justification for suppressing legitimate political debate or criticism, including criticism of the Commission itself,” he added. 

One of the key components of the event included research-driven lessons on three recently concluded elections in Sri Lanka. 

The results presented by Digital Democracy Research Officer Camila Weinmann and Digital Research Analyst Prihesh Ratnayake revealed that 66 accounts impersonated political parties and candidates on TikTok. 45.5% of accounts had been active during the 2024 Presidential Election and 21.2% of them remained active till the 2025 Local Council Election. In terms of action, following reports of these accounts made to TikTok and the ECSL, 51 of these accounts were removed. 

The research also revealed that women politicians faced higher levels of technology facilitated gender-based violence (TFGBV) during the 2024-2025 election cycle. The findings also revealed how chatbots spread inaccurate electoral information and how political advertisements kept running through the silence period during the Parliamentary Elections campaign. The research also shed light on Generative AI and risks to electoral integrity. 

The event also featured two panel discussions with panellists representing the media, ECSL, advocacy groups, and civil society. The first panel discussion, titled ‘The Election Information Ecosystem,’ discussed disinformation, accountability, and challenges to electoral integrity.

The first panel spoke about protocols that traditional newsrooms could follow when public figures make unverified claims and the effectiveness of counter-narratives in the form of drama, podcasts, and interviews. Panellists also discussed whether voluntary codes of conduct and Memorandums of Understanding between the ECSL and tech platforms are effective in countering disinformation, the legislative backing such institutions require, and rising polarisation as a main threat to information integrity.

The second panel discussion, titled ‘Resilience in Practice,’ drew experiences from fact-checking, advocacy, and media literacy work. The discussion navigated challenges when it comes to verifying information, type of responses received from social media companies during the fact-checking processes, how local journalists have been capacitated to counter disinformation, and lack of interest towards funding fact-checking initiatives.

Closing the event, DRI Project Manager Aingkaran Kugathasan thanked participants and partners for their contribution to the project. 

The event was held as part of the ‘Strengthening Resilience Against Disinformation in Sri Lanka’ project, co-funded by the European Union, and brought together representatives from international partner organisations, stakeholder institutions, the media, and civil society groups.

DRI and Factum produced eight research reports under the project. The reports are available at https://democracy-reporting.org/en/office/sri-lanka.

Asoka Goonetilleke

Asoka Goonetilleke commenced his journalistic career in Lake House in 1976 and after serving on the Central News Desk and in the foreign news desk, he left in 1982. Among them - An Adventurous Voyage to the Sea (Mahamuhuda Meda -Maranaya Abhiyasa), and The Black Dragon (Kalu Makara). He has also translated books from Sinhala language to English language - What Makes the Buddha Great, Impermanence in Plain English – both books were written by The Most Rev. Henepola Gunaratane.

He has been a lecturer and served in the National Olympic Committee of Sri Lanka, School of Sports Sciences (Sports Ministry) National Course Director - Sri Lanka and the International Olympic Committee. He has also worked at the Department of Govt. Information.

Goonetilleke has also received several awards. Among them Sports Journalist of the year 2000 (Editors Guild of Sri Lanka), Olympic Award for Excellence in Sports Journalism 2024 (International Olympic Committee), Presidential Award 2015 for the most outstanding sports publication, Kreeda Sahithya Vedi (2020-Sabuddhi Sports Literary Awards) and Multi Literal Sports Literate Award (2022- Sabuddhi Sports Literary Awards).

Anura Bandara Rajaguru 

Anura Bandara Rajaguru is a past student of Ananda College, Colombo, who commenced his journalistic career in Lake House in 1980 working for the Janatha and Yovun Janatha newspapers and subsequently joined the editorial teams of Silumina and Kreeda, after which he joined the Central News Desk before moving to the Navayugaya and Sarasaviya culminating in over four decades of work. Alongside his journalistic career, he built a parallel career in broadcasting, television, and writing.

1994, was a water-shed year in his career in journalism, while in Lake House he became the Deputy Editor of a new evening Sinhala language newspaper - Colombo Puwath and later Associate Editor of the newspaper. His contributions to creative writing earned him the Wimalasiri Perera Memorial Award for Creative Writing. He also completed a UNESCO course on writing for Children.

Chandra Fernando

After working under the leadership of S. T. Sivanayagam, she joined Sudamani, a newspaper launched by the Gunasena family, where she served as an Assistant Editor.

Fernando joined the Virakesari weekly edition as an assistant editor in 1997, during the period when Chandrika Subramaniam was in charge of the Virakesari weekly edition, she later worked as an Assistant Editor at Sudar Oli for a period before rejoining Virakesari. Rohan Abeywardena

In the run up to and after the signing of the Indo-Lanka Accord in July 1987, he manned the ‘hot seat’ of the News Editor in The Island, Sunday Island, The Sunday Times (twice). Abeywardena also had some memorable attachments with the Daily Mirror as Deputy Editor News at its launch and as the Associate Editor of the now defunct The Nation between 2003 and 2010. He also served as the editor of the Weekend Standard, when Tiran Alles launched that newspaper in 2006. 

He never bothered about hogging the limelight with his byline, but he ensured that journalists serving under him got as much exposure as possible. Till he retired in 2011, he was always in the thick of the news while keeping his reporters on their toes in the interest of the country whatever the personal consequences.

Since retirement he has continued to serve The Island online.

Ariyaratne Ganegoda

During his journalism career, he worked for the Aththa (1966–1990), Dinamina (1990–2005), Lankadeepa (2006–2011), and Mawbima (2018–2020) newspapers. Senior journalists Sirilal Kodikara, B.A. Siriwardena, Ariyawansa Pathiraja, and Bennet Rupasinghe are among his contemporaries.

title: Significant Court victory for Friends of Manipay Hospital in Ride For Ceylon dispute | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 05:19
-     - 23

Friends of Manipay Hospital (FOMH), a UK-registered charity supporting Green Memorial Hospital in Manipay, Sri Lanka, issuing a statement welcomed the order delivered by the Commercial High Court of Colombo on 7 October in Case No. CHC/014/2026/IP.

It said the Court rejected the applications for interim injunctions brought by a former volunteer rider against FOMH and other defendants, with an award of costs of Rs. 75,000.

“The decision represents a significant development in FOMH’s efforts to protect the Ride For Ceylon charitable fundraising initiative and its associated intellectual property interests,” FOMH said.

Following are excerpts from its statement. 

In its judgement, the Court acknowledged that the Ride For Ceylon name and mark had been used for a considerable period in fundraising activities undertaken by FOMH in both the UK and Sri Lanka.

The Court considered the history of the charitable cycling initiative, the involvement of volunteers, the competing claims to the trademark, and the evidence presented by the parties.

The judgement also recorded that the plaintiff was a volunteer member of FOMH and had participated in charitable fundraising activities undertaken for the benefit of Green Memorial Hospital.

The Court concluded that the plaintiff had not established sufficient grounds to prevent the defendants from continuing to use the Ride For Ceylon name and mark by way of the interim injunctions sought until the final determination of the case.

The Sri Lankan Court’s order also considered the earlier UK Intellectual Property Office (UK IPO) proceedings concerning the Ride For Ceylon trademark.

In decision O/882/22 dated 11 October 2022, the UK IPO upheld FOMH’s challenge to a similar attempt by another volunteer member and gave a decision on the Ride For Ceylon UK trademark ownership dispute in favour of the charity.

The Sri Lankan Commercial High Court noted that the plaintiff had knowledge of the UK IPO proceedings but had failed to disclose their status in the present action.

FOMH considers the UK IPO decision an important part of the documentary history establishing the charitable origins and ownership of the Ride For Ceylon brand in the UK.

Ride For Ceylon has brought together cyclists, sponsors, donors, and volunteers internationally to support the development of Green Memorial Hospital, a historic medical institution founded in 1848.

FOMH recognises and values the contributions made by volunteers over many years.

The charity nevertheless considers it essential that intellectual property, goodwill, and fundraising initiatives developed for charitable purposes remain protected for their intended beneficiaries.

FOMH will continue to act through its legal representatives to safeguard its interests and consider any further remedies advised by its legal team, including a possible claim in reconvention.

Legal costs incurred in protecting the assets, as well as travel costs to attend Court hearings, are personally met by the Trustees, without dissipating the charity’s funds.

The Board of Trustees of Friends of Manipay Hospital welcomes the Commercial High Court of Colombo’s decision.

The Trustees reaffirm their commitment to protecting the charitable purpose of Ride For Ceylon, maintaining public confidence in international fundraising and ensuring that the initiative continues to support healthcare services at Green Memorial Hospital.

The charity’s priority remains delivering lasting benefits to patients and other good causes recommended by its riders.

title: Are tax concessions really best way to attract investment to Sri Lanka? | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 04:27
-     - 22

A 25-year exemption by the Port City Economic Commission for a modest initial investment requires clear justification, and the resulting domestic employment, investment and economic activity must be proportionate to the revenue forgone

By Advocata Institute

Attracting foreign investment is a priority for Sri Lanka as it seeks to strengthen growth, create jobs and expand exports. Yet the growing reliance on tax concessions deserves reconsideration. Preferential tax treatment can encourage some investments, but it carries a fiscal cost, creates disparities between businesses and does not guarantee the benefits Governments expect.

Tax concessions are revenue foregone that could fund public services and infrastructure or reduce borrowing. They also tilt the playing field towards selected businesses. The central question is not how much investment a concession attracts, but whether that investment would have come anyway and whether the benefits justify the revenue forgone.

FThe long-term costs of generous investment incentives

Strategic investments still need to justify their tax benefits

The Colombo Port City illustrates these concerns. It already enjoys significant locational, infrastructural and regulatory advantages, including proximity to Colombo’s financial districts, modern infrastructure, planned airport expressway connectivity and a more flexible labour framework. Additional tax concessions on top of these raise questions about necessity and justification.

Concessions to port terminal operators also warrant scrutiny. Sri Lanka’s location on major East-West shipping routes is its ‘oil in the ground’, and the Port of Colombo has been an established maritime hub for over a century. Granting terminal operators tax holidays of up to 25 years raises the question of whether the country is capturing the full value of its strategic location.

Colombo West International Terminal Ltd., which operates the West Container Terminal, received a 25-year corporate income tax exemption under the Strategic Development Projects Act through a Government-to-Government arrangement rather than an open tender. Colombo International Container Terminals (CICT), which operates the South Terminal and was chosen through competitive tender, also enjoys a 25-year tax holiday. Private investment and expertise are valuable, but the Government must ask whether the scale and duration of these concessions are proportionate, given that modern port operations are highly automated and generate limited direct employment.

Tax concessions should not be granted simply because an investment is large. The Government must establish what additional benefits it will generate and whether they justify the fiscal cost.

The long-term costs of generous investment incentives

Generous incentives granted under earlier regimes can create lasting advantages for beneficiary companies. Long-standing concessions under Section 17 of the Board of Investment (BOI) Law, with tax-free periods followed by extended preferential rates, illustrate this.

According to their financial statements, Overseas Realty (Ceylon) PLC, Dialog Axiata PLC and Mobitel Ltd., received 15-year tax exemptions under BOI agreements signed in 2005, 1997 and 1994. After these expired in 2020, 2012 and 2009, each became eligible for a 2% tax on turnover for a further 15 years. These arrangements end in 2035 for Overseas Realty and 2027 for Dialog, while Mobitel’s expired in 2024.

Such investments may generate wider benefits through employment and related activity, but these must be weighed against the scale and duration of the relief. Long-term concessions should not continue by default and should be reviewed periodically to confirm that the intended benefits have materialised.

Selective concessions for real estate raise similar concerns. Havelock City Ltd., received a 15-year income tax exemption under a 2016 BOI agreement, while many other commercial developments proceeded without one. Several residential developers in the Port City, including Prime Melwa Port City Ltd., Home Lands Port City Ltd., Marina Hotel Holdings Ltd., and ICC Port City Ltd., have received substantial exemptions and incentives unavailable to comparable projects elsewhere. This disadvantages competitors and raises questions about the criteria for qualifying.

 The concern is sharper, where incentives support luxury developments that largely cater to wealthier buyers and rely heavily on imported materials and fittings. With Sri Lanka needing to strengthen its external position, the Government should ask whether import-intensive property is the best use of tax concessions, judging cases by their employment, foreign exchange earnings and economic linkages rather than the scale of investment.

 More broadly, differential tax treatment distorts resource allocation. Capital and labour should flow to where they generate the greatest returns to society, but preferential rates raise the after-tax returns of favoured activities relative to others, even when they are not the most productive. The wider the variation in effective tax rates, the greater the inefficiency.

The Port City BPO Ltd., received a 25-year tax holiday for an initial investment of $ 500,000 with a commitment to create 2,500 jobs within five years. Employment is an important justification, but it matters whether these jobs go to the domestic workforce. Recent reports that over 14,300 foreign worker visas have been issued under the Port City framework raise questions about who benefits. This highlights the need for greater transparency and monitoring by the Colombo Port City Economic Commission (CPEC) to ensure commitments are met. A 25-year exemption for a modest initial investment requires clear justification, and the resulting domestic employment, investment and economic activity must be proportionate to the revenue forgone.

The Inland Revenue Act also provides a 150% enhanced capital allowance for investments exceeding $ 3 million, rising to 200% in the Northern Province. Although intended to encourage capital formation, this may favour capital-intensive projects without generating much employment, as with renewable energy investments in the North, where natural solar and wind advantages can attract substantial capital but create few direct jobs.

Sri Lanka should move towards a more targeted framework that rewards measurable outcomes. For example, tax credits could encourage net job creation, employee training and the recruitment of underrepresented groups, particularly women, aligning incentives with broader development and labour market goals.

Changing global tax rules strengthen the case for reform

Changes in the international tax environment strengthen the case for reform. Under Pillar Two of the OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) framework, large multinational groups with annual consolidated revenue of at least €750 million face a 15% global minimum effective tax rate. Where eligible companies pay lower effective rates in countries such as Sri Lanka, another jurisdiction may collect the difference as additional tax. Some concessions may therefore no longer deliver their intended benefits to the countries offering them.

Sri Lanka should therefore compete on fundamentals: policy stability, efficient public services, reliable infrastructure, a skilled workforce and predictable regulation, rather than preferential tax treatment.

This does not mean tax incentives have no role. They should be reserved for clear market failures that prevent socially beneficial investment. For instance, airport infrastructure in an underdeveloped area can support tourism, hospitality and related industries even if direct financial returns alone would not attract private investors. In such cases, support may bridge the gap between private and social returns. The form of support matters, however. Direct grants or tax credits with defined limits are preferable to broad concessions that can cause substantial, open-ended revenue losses. Tax concessions should be considered only after assessing whether a market failure exists and whether a more targeted, fiscally predictable alternative could achieve the same goal.

Strengthening the governance of tax incentives

Sri Lanka also needs stronger institutional oversight of how incentives are designed, approved and monitored. The IMF’s 2024 Governance Diagnostic Assessment recommends that the Department of Fiscal Policy play a central role in evaluating and guiding incentive design. Institutions such as the Board of Investment and the Colombo Port City Economic Commission may be better placed to assess commercial potential, but the fiscal implications of their decisions must be considered within the Government’s broader revenue priorities.

International experience offers examples. The Philippines has progressively reformed its framework through the Tax Incentives Management and Transparency Act of 2015, the CREATE Act of 2021 and the CREATE MORE Act of 2024. These provide central oversight through the Fiscal Incentives Review Board, cost-benefit analysis in approvals, and reporting requirements under which beneficiary firms disclose incentives received and outcomes such as investment, employment and exports. This makes fiscal costs and economic results visible and enables evaluation of whether incentives deliver.

Ultimately, success should not be measured by the volume of capital entering the country or the number of businesses receiving concessions, but by the quality of investment and its contribution to productive employment, productivity, technology transfer and broader economic activity. Sri Lanka needs an incentive framework that is transparent, targeted, time-bound and regularly evaluated, with clear evidence that the benefits outweigh the fiscal costs.

The objective should not be to offer investors the most generous tax concessions, but to create an environment in which investing in Sri Lanka is attractive even without them.

title: State and your hard-earned money: Moral contract  AKD cannot afford to ignore | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 04:13
-     - 84

President and Finance Minister delivering his second Budget in November 2025. His third Budget will be read in Parliament this Thursday (12) amid growing concern over high taxes and poor public services

The third Budget’s ultimate test will be neither the enthusiasm surrounding revenue achievements nor the generosity of promised concessions. It will be whether ordinary citizens believe they are treated fairly and their money is used responsibly. Failure to honour this moral contract could deepen dissent and undermine even worthwhile policies, including good-governance and anti-corruption programs

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s third Budget is approaching amid growing concern over high taxes and poor public services. The AKD Government, closely following International Monetary Fund (IMF) prescriptions, takes pride in exceeding revenue targets. Yet its satisfaction is not shared by many taxpayers, who question whether they receive value for the money they surrender to the State. Fiscal success means little to citizens unless it translates into better services and improved living conditions.

With the Opposition capitalising on these grievances, pressure for tax relief is mounting. AKD and his senior ministers have promised reductions in the forthcoming Budget without compromising revenue targets. The challenge is to turn these assurances into meaningful relief while preserving the hard-won gains in fiscal stability.

For guidance, AKD would do well to read Paolo Mauro’s recently published book, ‘The State and Your Hard-Earned Money’. Its subtitle, A Global Perspective on Morality and Public Finance, captures its relevance to Sri Lanka’s predicament. The former senior IMF economist explores two fundamental questions: how much of citizens’ earnings is the State morally entitled to collect, and what does it owe those who pay? These questions place the taxpayer, rather than the revenue target, at the centre of fiscal policy.

This is more than a book about taxation and expenditure. It examines the moral relationship between the State and its citizens, urging policymakers to look beyond fiscal targets and consider fairness, integrity and public purpose. Those preparing Sri Lanka’s next Budget should keep these principles firmly in view.

Taxation: More than a Government revenue exercise

Mauro begins with a fundamental question: what is the right thing to do when a Government collects and spends public money?

Taxation is usually debated in terms of revenue, deficits, debt sustainability and growth. Governments need resources to provide services, maintain infrastructure and meet social obligations. The need for taxation is rarely disputed; the harder questions are how much to collect, from whom and for what purposes.

Yet taxation is also a moral issue. Every rupee collected comes from income that individuals or businesses could otherwise spend, save or invest in education and better living standards. The State must therefore offer a convincing public justification for taking part of those earnings.

Citizens have a duty to contribute to the common good, and a functioning State requires adequate resources. But this obligation is reciprocal: the State’s authority to tax carries a corresponding responsibility to serve its people.

This is more than a book about taxation and expenditure. It examines the moral relationship between the State and its citizens, urging policymakers to look beyond fiscal targets and consider fairness, integrity and public purpose

Fairness: Who should pay and how much?

Mauro explores the growing concern over fairness in taxation and the distribution of income and wealth.

Different philosophical approaches emphasise different principles: contributing according to ability to pay, retaining the rewards of work and enterprise, and ensuring equal opportunities so that disadvantaged people are not excluded from the benefits of development.

These principles need not conflict. A fair tax system should recognise individual effort without placing a disproportionate burden on those least able to finance public services. Fairness requires balancing these concerns.

In Sri Lanka, taxes affect groups differently. Salaried employees taxed at source have little scope to avoid or defer payment, while small businesses face substantial compliance costs. Consumption taxes weigh especially heavily on lower-income households, which spend a larger share of their earnings on essentials. These differences matter when assessing who bears the burden of taxation and whether the system treats citizens fairly.

The test is not merely whether the Government raises enough revenue, but whether the burden is shared fairly. Fairness does not require cutting every tax or shielding wealthy individuals and profitable businesses from higher contributions. It requires a system citizens can understand and accept.

AKD’s forthcoming Budget should therefore target genuine inequities and ease disproportionate burdens, rather than use tax relief to reward selected groups for political advantage. Fairness, not favouritism, should guide relief.

The expanding State and the quality of public services

Mauro examines the State’s expanding role. Beyond law and order and basic administration, modern governments are responsible for education, healthcare, transport, infrastructure and social protection.

These obligations require more revenue, but also demand greater efficiency and accountability. A larger State must demonstrate that it uses public money well.

Sri Lankan taxpayers’ frustration is therefore understandable. Despite paying income taxes, VAT and other levies, they face difficulties in public hospitals, poorly resourced schools, inadequate transport and neglected infrastructure. Public institutions are frequently criticised for delays, inefficiency and indifference to citizens’ needs.

Not all these failures originated with the present Government. It inherited serious economic and institutional problems, limited fiscal space, heavy debt obligations and competing demands. Nevertheless, its performance must be judged by the services it delivers, not simply the revenue it collects.

Fiscal consolidation cannot indefinitely justify high taxes while the quality of public services remains inadequate. Taxpayers deserve tangible benefits in return for their contributions.

The next Budget must therefore be assessed not only against revenue targets and the IMF’s primary-balance requirement, but also against visible improvements in daily life. The State must learn to spend as carefully as it collects: fiscal discipline and better services must advance together.

Corruption: The enemy of the taxpayer

Corruption is among the most important issues Mauro examines, particularly for Sri Lanka. He explores why it persists and how institutional opportunities and incentives enable public resources to be diverted for private gain.

The damage extends beyond missing money: corruption undermines the relationship between the State and its citizens.

An ordinary taxpayer works hard, pays taxes and expects that money to serve the public. Inflated contracts, wasteful spending, political patronage and outright theft betray that expectation. The sense of injustice deepens when those responsible escape accountability. Taxpayers are entitled to feel cheated when their contributions enrich private interests rather than meet public needs.

Corruption also fuels a destructive cycle. Perceived misuse of public money weakens willingness to pay taxes and makes evasion and avoidance more socially acceptable. Falling compliance then prompts stricter enforcement or higher rates, further increasing resentment.

Fighting corruption is therefore not separate from sound public finance. It is essential to sustaining a tax system that citizens trust and are willing to support.

For the AKD Government, elected on a strong mandate for good governance and ending corruption, the stakes are particularly high. Its anti-corruption program is more than a political pledge: it is essential to restoring public trust in the State.

Citizens asked to sacrifice for economic recovery must see public officials held equally accountable. The Government must uphold one law for everyone, award contracts transparently and act against those who misuse public funds, without political interference or favouritism.

Once taxpayers lose confidence, securing cooperation for necessary reforms becomes much harder. Public trust is therefore not an optional benefit of sound fiscal policy; it is vital to its success. Mauro’s lesson is simple: the State must earn the trust of those whose money it collects.

The IMF program and the Government’s responsibility

Sri Lanka’s IMF program is central to its economic recovery. Following the crisis, restoring fiscal discipline, rebuilding foreign reserves and reducing public debt became unavoidable priorities.

The Government deserves credit for maintaining discipline and exceeding programme targets. According to the IMF’s 2026 review, total revenue reached 16.6% of GDP in 2025, against an estimate of 14.6%. Tax revenue was 15.4%, compared with a 13.6% target. The primary surplus reached 5.4%, well above the 2.3% target.

Yet the sources of this overperformance matter. The IMF attributes much of the revenue increase to surging motor vehicle imports and related taxes, while noting that capital expenditure fell below budgeted levels.

Exceptional import receipts do not necessarily signal a lasting improvement in the tax system. Nor does a surplus achieved partly by underspending on capital projects demonstrate better financial management. Collecting more while postponing essential infrastructure and development investment cannot secure long-term prosperity. Fiscal results must therefore be assessed for their durability and the expenditure choices behind them, not celebrated solely for exceeding targets.

The IMF recommends stronger tax administration, a broader tax base, rationalised exemptions and a medium-term revenue strategy to improve efficiency and equity. These reforms provide a framework for recovery, not a substitute for the Government’s judgement. Within that framework, elected leaders must make choices reflecting Sri Lanka’s social and moral priorities. They remain responsible for explaining unpopular decisions and ensuring that public money serves citizens. The IMF should neither become a blanket excuse for fiscal decisions nor a scapegoat for domestic failures in administration, expenditure management or service delivery.

The moral contract between State and citizen

Mauro’s most valuable contribution is his insistence that fiscal policy must draw on broader moral perspectives. Citizens judge taxation not simply by calculations, but by fairness, officials’ conduct, public services and the opportunities available to their families. They may accept higher taxes when public money is used honestly and efficiently, yet resent even modest levies when it is wasted or institutions appear corrupt and indifferent. The legitimacy of taxation therefore depends not only on what the State collects, but also on how it behaves and what it delivers.

This is the moral contract between the State and the citizen. Citizens contribute to common objectives; in return, the State provides security, essential services, equal treatment, economic opportunities and governance that protects the public interest. Neither side’s responsibilities can be considered in isolation. The contract is more than an abstract ideal: it should shape budget priorities, spending decisions and everyday administration. It links the citizen’s duty to pay with the Government’s duty to justify the use of that money. Revenue collection and public service are thus reciprocal obligations, not separate exercises.

For Sri Lanka, fulfilling this contract means practising good governance: collecting revenue fairly, spending prudently and accounting transparently. Public institutions must serve citizens rather than political or private interests. Decisions must be explained, officials held accountable and corruption rejected. The Government must also listen to grievances and revise policies that cause unnecessary hardship. The AKD Government has repeatedly pledged good governance and action against corruption. It must now translate those promises into the management of public finances. The forthcoming Budget should make the moral contract an explicit guiding principle, connecting fiscal decisions with citizens’ expectations of fairness and responsible Government.

What should the next Budget deliver?

The next Budget gives AKD an opportunity to move beyond celebrating revenue targets and address citizens’ legitimate concerns through six priorities.

Fiscal discipline and social justice need not conflict. A well-designed Budget should advance both, making public finances sustainable while ensuring that citizens receive fair treatment and tangible value for their contributions.

The forthcoming Budget gives AKD an opportunity to turn that principle into practice. He should seize it before frustration becomes a deeper crisis of confidence, placing responsible stewardship at the heart of fiscal policy. The State may have the power to collect our hard-earned money. But it has a moral obligation to earn the right to spend it

A Budget that restores trust

Mauro’s book reminds us that successful public finance cannot be measured by revenue alone. A Government may meet fiscal targets, record a primary surplus and satisfy international creditors without winning its citizens’ confidence. Economic recovery must ultimately improve people’s lives. Fiscal stability is essential to that goal, but it is a means, not an end. The distinction matters when judging a Budget that asks citizens to make sacrifices.

AKD can use the forthcoming Budget to renew the relationship between the State and the taxpayer through fair taxation, efficient spending, integrity and accountability. Tax relief should not be a political concession to silence the Opposition, but part of a broader effort to make Government more responsive and responsible. Citizens, too, must recognise that taxation sustains essential services, supports recovery and protects future generations from excessive debt. The goal is not a State without taxes, but one that justifies what it collects. Both sides must honour their obligations if this relationship is to endure.

The third Budget’s ultimate test will be neither the enthusiasm surrounding revenue achievements nor the generosity of promised concessions. It will be whether ordinary citizens believe they are treated fairly and their money is used responsibly. Failure to honour this moral contract could deepen dissent and undermine even worthwhile policies, including good-governance and anti-corruption programs. Once taxpayers lose confidence, securing cooperation for necessary reforms becomes much harder. Public trust is therefore not an optional benefit of sound fiscal policy; it is vital to its success.

Mauro’s lesson is simple: the State must earn the trust of those whose money it collects. The forthcoming Budget gives AKD an opportunity to turn that principle into practice. He should seize it before frustration becomes a deeper crisis of confidence, placing responsible stewardship at the heart of fiscal policy.

The State may have the power to collect our hard-earned money. But it has a moral obligation to earn the right to spend it.
